visible.summary: Malawi is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years) AND Human Dignity Trust lists Malawi as criminalising the gender expression of trans people. A moratorium on prosecutions has held since 2014, but in June 2024 the Constitutional Court upheld the ban — a case brought partly by a local trans woman and her Dutch partner — and religious leaders led nationwide anti-LGBT marches in 2023. Discrimination and violence are regular despite the moratorium.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 14 years, moratorium since 2014) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the moratorium is informal and revocable.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Prosecution moratorium is informal and revocable; the 2024 ruling keeps the statute fully alive.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch dispatch (11 July 2024): Malawi's Constitutional Court on 28 June 2024 rejected the challenge to Penal Code sections 153, 154 and 156 — a three-member panel dismissed the application brought by Dutch national Jan Willen Akster and Jana Gonani, a trans woman who received an eight-year sentence in a men's prison in December 2021. The sections carry up to 14 years' imprisonment; faith-based groups filed briefs and religious leaders led nationwide protests claiming the case sought to legalise same-sex marriage. The court left any reform to parliament; HRW called it a 'dark day' and warned of heightened arbitrary-arrest and violence risks.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Malawi: documents the July 2011 protest killings (20 dead), harsh prisons, and 'discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) persons'.

Human Rights Watch (26 October 2018), releasing the 61-page report 'Let Posterity Judge' based on interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre plus lawyers, activists and officials: police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people, sometimes assaulting them, and medical staff denied services on gender-expression grounds (a trans man beaten then refused treatment; nurses mocked people presenting for HIV tests). Men face up to 14 years and women five years under sections 153/156; the 2012 justice-minister moratorium on arrests was reaffirmed in December 2015 but suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016 after religious leaders' litigation, leaving its legality contested. People whose gender expression differs from expectations are 'most likely to be targeted'.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 December 2015): two men arrested in Malawi on 7 December on homosexuality charges suffered house ransacking and assault by neighbours, threats of being burned alive, attempted extortion and humiliation by community police — forced stripping, forced medical and HIV/STD examinations, and photos distributed on social media. CEDEP's Gift Trapence contrasts the arrests with government Global Fund money for LGBTI HIV services. Documents the arrest-and-abuse pattern under the penal code.

Erasing 76 Crimes (27 April 2018): police arrested Limbani Sibande, 24, in Mzuzu for suspected homosexuality and charged him under section 156 ('indecent practices between males') rather than section 153 — apparently to circumvent the six-year moratorium on anti-gay arrests while both laws faced a constitutional challenge. Police spokespersons confirmed the custody. Evidence of law-enforcement attempts to elude the moratorium.

visible.summary:
Sudan is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Article 152 of the Penal Code criminalises gender nonconformity directly; sodomy carries life imprisonment (capital/corporal punishment removed in 2020 reforms); and Cairo 52 documents state violence against LGBTQIA+ people including extrajudicial killings. Since April 2023 the country has been in a catastrophic civil war (SAF vs RSF) with documented mass atrocities — the conflict intensifies every risk and eliminates any recourse. There is no LGR and no community infrastructure.

For a visitor: statutory criminalisation of gender nonconformity plus one of the world's worst active conflicts.
visible.tangentialFactors: Sodomy carries life imprisonment — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: War conditions affect all; Art 152 is trans-specific.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 Sudan profile: penal code Article 152 criminalises wearing clothing of the opposite sex (cross-dressing provisions); no arrest statistics for trans people but documented state violence including extrajudicial killings against LGBTQIA+ individuals; no legal gender recognition, gender-affirming healthcare legally constrained, the ongoing conflict further restricts access, and state reliance on Sunni fatwas blocks transition. Gender-nonconformity framing for visitor risk.

Human Dignity Trust country profile: Sudan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, with sentences including a maximum of life imprisonment (and historically the death penalty for a third offence). (Only the opening was retrievable at fetch time.)

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Sudan: documents the Bashir regime's abuses - extrajudicial killings, torture, Darfur conflict, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation under Article 148 with flogging and death penalty provisions.

Berkouwer, Sultan & Yehia (2014): 'Homosexuality in Sudan and Egypt: Stories of the Struggle for Survival' - by a Harvard research fellow with activists of Bedayaa (the LGBTQI organisation for the Nile Valley); explores daily struggles, discrimination and violence rooted in societal gender and sexual norms, and whether post-Arab-Spring change will transform circumstances.

Rainbow Sudan — Sudan's community magazine: runs sections on LGBTI rights in Sudan (history and analysis), a profile of Sudan and LGBTI organisations, i.e. documents an organised local community presence. Landing/index page: thin for current findings.

76crimes (15 Jul 2020): Sudan's Sovereign Council removed the death penalty for homosexuality — maximum now life imprisonment for a third offence — abolished the 100 lashes for same-sex intimacy, and set up to five years' imprisonment for a first offence in the criminal-code amendment.

visible.summary:
South Sudan is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The 2008 Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years), and Human Dignity Trust lists South Sudan as criminalising the gender expression of trans people. The country has barely emerged from civil war, state institutions are vestigial outside Juba, communal violence is endemic, and there is no documented LGBT community infrastructure whatsoever — no organisation can operate openly. No trans-specific case is documented because documentation itself is nearly impossible.

For a visitor: statutory risk plus a near-total absence of protective institutions.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 14 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Documentation absence reflects state incapacity; gender-expression criminalisation is statutory.

visible.summary:
Somalia is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — one of the world's most dangerous countries for any LGBT person. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 3 years), but the operative reality is worse: Al-Shabaab controls significant territory and applies its interpretation of sharia, under which homosexuality and gender transgression are capital offences — executions are documented. Even in government areas, mob violence and clan-justice dynamics make any gender nonconformity lethal-risk. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, and no recourse of any kind.

For a visitor: there is no safe way to be visibly trans anywhere in Somalia.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 3 years) and capital under Al-Shabaab's sharia — a catastrophic exposure for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Fragmented authority means enforcement varies; Al-Shabaab areas apply capital punishment.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Somalia's criminalisation of same-sex sexual activity (up to life imprisonment under the 1964 penal code; death penalty under Sharia in some regions).

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Somalia: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 3 years); al-Shabaab enforces strict Sharia with death as possible punishment; pervasive violence and statelessness.

US State Dept 2022 Country Report, Somalia: criminalizes 'carnal intercourse with a person of the same sex', 3 months' to 3 years' imprisonment, no official reports of enforcement available; under local interpretations of sharia, homosexuality is punishable by death; no known state-conducted executions of that sort reported. Impunity generally remained the norm.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Somalia (archived): documents the conflict, al-Shabaab abuses, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and the death penalty under Islamic law in areas under insurgent control.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 Feb 2016) on Benjamin Christman's 'Report on the Treatment of Gay Persons in Somalia' (published 2 Feb 2016): evidence that gay persons should not be returned to Somalia due to persecution risk, supporting refugee-status claims; notes Somalia's anti-homosexuality law provides up to... [report excerpt] — non-refoulement basis for LGBT asylum seekers.

Al Jazeera (Jul 2013) 'Gay Somali refugees face death threats': refugees in Kenya face threats and racist discrimination, with Al-Shabaab publicising intent to 'enforce harsh punishments' against homosexuality and senior figures claiming a 'death chamber' for gay and lesbians if returned; UN officials nevertheless pushed return — dated account of persecution driving displacement.

visible.summary: Eritrea is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Article 310(1) of the 2015 Penal Code criminalises “homosexual conduct” (up to 7 years), there are no anti-discrimination protections of any kind, and Eritrea is among the world's most closed states — indefinite national service, mass arbitrary detention, no independent media, no civil society, and no way to document conditions. Eritrea has rejected every SOGI recommendation at every UPR cycle. Nothing is known about trans people in Eritrea because nothing can be known — the absence of data reflects total informational control.
visible.tangentialFactors: Article 310(1) criminalises homosexual conduct (up to 7 years) — trans visitors are captured via birth-sex status.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Documentation absence reflects totalitarian informational control.

sources.claim: Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): Article 310(1) of the penal code criminalises 'homosexual conduct' with up to 7 years' imprisonment — inherited from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code and retained with an enhanced sentence in the first post-independence penal code (adopted 2015).

US State Dept 2023 Country Reports (Eritrea): Section 7 records that openly LGBTQI+ persons risked imprisonment and therefore did not participate in the political process; societal discrimination against LGBTQI+ persons continues alongside a law making no gender distinction for assault.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Eritrea (archived): documents the authoritarian regime's abuses - torture, arbitrary detention, indefinite national service - with the LGBT section noting criminalisation and societal stigma.

Asmarino relay of the US State Department 2011 human rights report on Eritrea: societal abuse and discrimination against gay men and lesbians occurred; the government labelled disloyal individuals 'gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles'; the law criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity.

UK Foreign Office 'Eritrea: Country of Concern' human rights report (© 2015): same-sex activity is a crime in Eritrea and there is no anti-discrimination legislation protecting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people; the UK raised these concerns bilaterally and via the EU.

visible.summary: Antigua and Barbuda demands real caution. The High Court struck down the buggery/gross-indecency laws in July 2022, reading the constitutional bar on sex discrimination to cover sexual orientation and gender identity. No LGR, no anti-discrimination statute, and residual social hostility; tourist resort areas are insulated.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2022 decriminalisation ruling covers same-sex conduct — relevant to trans visitors travelling with a partner; the criminal statutes no longer apply to anyone.
visible.localsOnly: No legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination statute — resident-facing gaps.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Decriminalisation is recent; social climate lags the courts.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (Jul 2022): 'Antigua and Barbuda: High Court Decriminalizes Gay Sex' — the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court strikes down the 'sodomy' and 'gross indecency' provisions.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): in 2022 the High Court found Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995 unconstitutional, decriminalising same-sex conduct, and interpreted 'sex' discrimination to include sexual orientation and gender identity. However, no explicit antidiscrimination protections exist, same-sex unions are not recognised, and trans people are particularly vulnerable because there is no mechanism to change legal gender markers - only name changes.

El País/AP (June 2023): profile of Orden David, the Antiguan LGBTQ activist who challenged the country's anti-sodomy law and won in 2022 - he had been bullied and physically attacked (struck in the head, knocked out in daylight); the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court ruled the law unconstitutional; six Caribbean countries still criminalise.

St Lucia Star (Dec 2019): ECADE announced court challenges to buggery and indecency laws in Barbados, St Kitts-Nevis, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and Saint Lucia, arguing the laws stigmatise and legitimise hate speech, discrimination and violence.

The Advocates for Human Rights (January 2025): submission to the UN Human Rights Committee for Antigua and Barbuda listing LGBTQ+ rights issues ahead of its review — documents the open SOGI-protection questions the state still faces post-2022 decriminalisation.
